title: A Service Is More Than an App
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: A Service Is More Than an App.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A service is a system of people, policies, processes, technology, environments, partners, and channels that together help someone achieve an outcome. Customers experience the promise across all of it, not according to an organisation chart.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Find the real unit of design
turns.text: What changes when we look at find the real unit of design?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The unit of service design is the outcome over time, not the channel or screen. To locate it, start with the event that creates the need and stop only when the outcome has been delivered, refused with a usable alternative, or safely concluded.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Then identify the people, organisations, policies, records, technology, money, locations, and time dependencies that make the outcome possible. This boundary is a working hypothesis: expand it when an unexplained failure originates outside the map.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The resulting service brief names a shared outcome—reach a suitable appointment and arrive prepared—plus guardrails for clinical safety, access, staff workload, and unresolved cases. Product metrics such as form completion remain useful diagnostics, but they cannot substitute for the service outcome. Ownership must cross the same boundary as the promise.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: account recovery?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A recovery screen may be perfectly usable while the service fails because identity records are outdated, agents lack authority, letters arrive late, or fraud rules exclude legitimate customers. Treating recovery as a whole service changes the design problem from “improve the code form” to “restore legitimate access safely across digital, phone, and assisted routes.”

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at define the service boundary?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Start with the outcome people seek and follow every actor, channel, rule, record, dependency, and time period required to produce it. Include preparation, waiting, staff work, suppliers, and recovery. The boundary is wide enough when the team can explain why the promise succeeds or fails, not merely what the interface displays.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Identify value exchange and burden. A digital shortcut may reduce organisational handling while shifting data entry, uncertainty, or repair to customers. Compare experience for people who cannot or do not use the app. Consistency means shared promise, status, and outcome across channels—not identical screens.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Assign ownership for the whole journey. Local product metrics can improve while the service worsens elsewhere. Use a shared outcome and guardrails for customer progress, staff work, access, and failure demand.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Design the outcome across the whole service
turns.text: What changes when we look at design the outcome across the whole service?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: He defines the service boundary from the user's perspective, including discovery, eligibility, waiting, handoff, completion, and recovery. Organisational boundaries remain visible as constraints but do not become excuses for experience gaps. A transfer that is effortless in the app but creates an unowned clinical review is not a successful service interaction.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: When a customer complaint crosses teams, keep the customer journey intact. Internal boundaries explain ownership; they do not excuse a broken promise.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The service boundary begins with the outcome a person is trying to achieve, not the digital channel a team owns. Include discovery, eligibility, onboarding, transaction, fulfilment, support, recovery, renewal, and exit where they matter. Map customers, staff, partners, systems, policy, data, places, and communications.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The customer may experience only a small visible surface while the outcome depends on many backstage decisions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: This perspective changes diagnosis. A confusing status screen may reflect an upstream system that cannot supply reliable status. A form that seems too long may be collecting evidence required by policy. A call-centre complaint may reveal a broken handoff rather than poor agent performance.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Design can improve the interface, but it must also make operational dependencies and trade-offs visible to the people who can change them.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Channel ownership: a team optimises its app while shifting work to another channel. Screen-level diagnosis: visible symptoms are fixed repeatedly while the cause persists backstage. Missing actor: staff, partner, or affected non-user work is absent from the model. Promise gap: marketing or UI promises an outcome operations cannot reliably provide.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A food-delivery app offers a perfect tracker, but the restaurant has no inventory, the courier cannot find the address, and support cannot issue a refund. The app is only one channel in the service.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Module 9 scaled product patterns. Service design scales the experience across channels and operations. lesson 56 defines the qualities that make a service understandable from the start.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Name every person and system involved in one food-delivery order, from intent to support after delivery.
